items.blurb: One of the challenges of searching for “technosignatures” (i.e. signs that intelligent life somewhere in the universe has created technology) is understanding what to look for. Technology is a very broad area, and different types would show up as different features. One of the most commonly cited is a Dyson sphere, which attempts to encapsulate a star and capture it’s outgoing light to produce energy. But while we’ve looked for the mid-infrared waste heat these structures would produce for decades, we haven’t found a definitive instance of one. According to a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv by Turkish high school student Sahin Torlakcik, that might be because we are looking for the wrong type of energy all together.

items.title: A Germinal Center-Independent Innate-Like Memory B Cell Compartment of B1 Origin
items.blurb: Memory B cells (MBCs) are a critical cellular reservoir for long-term humoral immunity. MBCs display heterogeneous isotypes and surface markers and can arise through both germinal center (GC)-dependent and GC-independent extrafollicular (EF) pathways. Both the mechanisms controlling EF MBC differentiation and the identities of the B cell populations from which EF MBCs derive remain poorly understood. To capture MBC diversity, we applied a broad selection strategy followed by transcriptional profiling, identifying a subset of MBCs characterized by minimal class switching, limited somatic hypermutation, and an innate-like gene signature. Using genetic models, we demonstrated that this subset arises independently of GC responses and derives from innate B1 cells. These innate-like MBCs differentiate into antigen-specific antibody-secreting cells and confer protection against lethal viral infection. Together, our findings define a previously unrecognized arm of MBC responses, demonstrating that innate B1 cells contribute a non-redundant antibody repertoire to protective immunological memory.

items.title: Modeling Parkinsonian Freezing and Deep Brain Stimulation Effects in a Basal Ganglia Network
items.blurb: he precise mechanism through which Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) mitigates freezing episodes in Parkinson's disease remains unknown. We modelled Parkinsonian freezing using a model of the basal ganglia that adopts a Dynamic Neural Field network for simultaneous action selection (selecting emph{which} action is executed) and specification (resolving the continuous parameters governing emph{how} that action is performed). Action selection success was based on whether activation surpassed a threshold. The model robustly differentiated healthy and dopamine-depleted (Parkinsonian) conditions, producing stable action selection under healthy dopamine and impaired, freeze-prone dynamics following depletion. We then modelled DBS as a scaled reduction in afferent drive to the subthalamic nucleus and globus pallidus internus. While this formulation has succeeded in previous computational work, it did not yield consistent restoration of action selection within our framework, motivating future investigation of alternative DBS formulations.

items.title: Anti-Z-NA antibodies can distinguish accessible Z-form states across DNA, RNA, and DNA-RNA substrates
items.blurb: Left-handed (Z-form) double-stranded nucleic acid conformers (Z-DNA and Z-RNA, collectively called Z-NA) are molecular patterns recognized by ADAR1 and ZBP1, which are sensor proteins involved in innate immunity. Monoclonal antibodies raised against Z-DNA, such as Z22 and Z-D11, are employed as probes for the study of Z-NAs, but their substrate specificity and functional equivalence remain unclear. Here, we used biochemical, biophysical, and structural approaches to compare the binding modes and target specificies of Z22 and Z-D11, using Z-prone CG-rich dsDNA, dsRNA, and DNA-RNA hybrids as substrates. Both antibodies failed to form stable complexes with short CG-rich dsRNA under conditions compatible with antibody stability, which suggests that they are unable to induce A-to-Z transitions in dsRNA. In contrast, both antibodies robustly complexed with dsDNA and DNA-RNA hybrid substrates. Cryo-EM structural analysis confirmed that both antibodies interact with Z-NA through a conserved interaction network, and demonstrated that complexes between the antibodies and DNA-RNA hybrids adopted distinct higher-order organizations. Z22 retained binding to both Z-DNA and Z-RNA segments, whereas Z-D11 displayed substrate-dependent organization and was restricted to Z-DNA segments Molecular modelling provided mechanistic explanation for the differences in Z-RNA binding ability between the two antibodies, which was confirmed in situ with ADAR1-depleted, IAV-infected and JTE607-treated cells. We also demonstrate that Z-D11, in contrast to previously described Z22, is unable to induce B-to-Z-transitions in short d(CG)6 oligos under physiological conditions. Together, these results show that anti Z-NA monoclonal antibodies are not functionally interchangeable: whereas Z22 recognizes pre-formed Z-RNA, Z-DNA-RNA hybrids, and Z-DNA, Z-D11 recognizes Z-DNA, and DNA segments in Z-DNA-RNA hybrids. These differences are dictated by substrate composition, local geometry, and conformational accessibility, which also likely impact their ability to induce NA structural transitions. These findings have important implications for interpreting antibody-based detection of left-handed nucleic acids in biological systems.

The collapse of the rules-based order is not confined to the land: we’re imperilled as centuries of maritime cooperation sink beneath the waves

The US military campaign to protect merchant shipping from Iranian attacks by asserting direct maritime control in the strait of Hormuz is not an idea unique to Donald Trump’s administration. Almost exactly 200 years ago, in the period 1825-27, a powerful US naval squadron led by Commodore John Rodgers was sent to the Mediterranean to defend American ships from the depredations of Greek corsairs and pirates.

For all the new-minted republic’s brave talk of liberty, the US squadron did not assist Greece’s ongoing “regime change” struggle for independence from the Ottoman empire. Its sole, self-serving purpose was to defend US trade, markets and business interests. After abandoning his call for a people’s revolution in Tehran, this, too, is what Trump’s reckless war with Iran has now boiled down to.

items.title: Electrolyte lemonade to probiotic pop: do the new generation of ‘functional drinks’ live up to the hype?
items.blurb:
They make grand claims about beauty benefits or extra energy – and even actor Gillian Anderson has her own brand. We investigate what they’re really doing – and put them to a taste test

Show yourself some love. Fuel your focus. Life’s too good for bad energy. Find your calm in the everyday chaos. Live fit. No, not new-age slogans or something you’d find scribbled in neon on the wall of a cocktail bar, but marketing taglines slapped across cans of functional soft drinks. Walk into any supermarket or newsagent and there they are, bright and cheerful, right next to the Tango, promising everything from improved mental clarity and zen-like calm, to a blast of highly caffeinated energy as part of your sandwich-and-a-snack lunchtime meal deal. Influencers love them. Your favourite podcasters are sponsored by them. Even Gillian Anderson has a functional drinks brand (brilliantly, she’s called it G Spot).

If you have not yet swigged an electrolyte-loaded lemonade or opened a can of probiotic fizzy pop, you might be wondering what functional drinks even are. Because they are marketed as having one or more of many possible physiological and cognitive benefits, it’s a big category. There are functional drinks for focus, productivity, relaxation, calm, protein, energy, gut health and perhaps most confusingly, for hydration – which is, after all, the core function of most potable liquids.

The recent retirement of Macquarie Group CEO Shemara Wikramanayake marks the culmination of a highly successful career. She’s leaving the company with shares worth hundreds of millions of dollars after nearly 40 years at the Sydney-based institution. Under her leadership, the “millionaires’ factory” has increased its annual revenue by around 80% and nearly doubled its profit. Wikramanayake has also overseen and consolidated the group’s transition from a firm specialising in privatised infrastructure to a global merchant bank earning profits from commodity trading, specialist asset finance and wealth management.

Macquarie shareholders, who have tripled their money over the past eight years (with dividends and capital gains), have plenty of reason to be grateful.

Its demise is also the consequence of the relentless application of a neo-liberal political philosophy that for years has elevated financial engineering above real engineering; off-balance-sheet finance above paying for things openly; and lauded the private sector above the public sector.

items.blurb: “When I was a child, every highway journey meant stopping at a petrol pump to clean insects off the windscreen. There were so many of them that everyone did it. Children today will probably never know what that looked like. It’s one of the best reminders of how much we have lost,” says Sohail Madan. For 43-year-old Sohail, that childhood memory is more than nostalgia. It reminds him of a time when butterflies , moths, bees and birds were such an ordinary part of daily life that nobody imagined they could disappear. Today, as founder and director of WildTales Foundation, Sohail has spent over 15 years helping bring nature back to forests, neighbourhoods and school campuses. His work has ranged from restoring damaged landscapes and growing native plants to creating butterfly corridors across Delhi. Ask him where conservation begins, and his answer is surprisingly simple. “People think conservation only happens inside forests or wildlife sanctuaries. But every balcony, every terrace and every backyard can become part of the solution.” His words come at a time when scientists are warning that wildlife around us is quietly disappearing. The State of India's Birds 2023 report found that nearly half the bird species assessed are showing long-term declines, with around 178 species now considered to be of conservation concern. Around the world, studies have also documented sharp declines in insect populations, driven largely by habitat loss and excessive chemical use. For Sohail, however, this isn't just about numbers in a report. It is something he has witnessed first-hand. Many people remember childhood afternoons chasing butterflies through gardens, waking up to birdsong or watching moths gather around porch lights after the first summer rain. Today, those everyday sights have become noticeably rarer. Rather than simply worrying about the loss, Sohail decided to do something about it. A childhood fascination that became a calling Long before he began restoring habitats, nature had already shaped his life. Born in Africa, where his parents worked as doctors, Sohail spent his early years surrounded by wildlife. Even after the family moved to Delhi, weekends outdoors and visits to nearby forests kept that fascination alive. Today, as founder and director of WildTales Foundation, Sohail has spent over 15 years helping bring nature back to forests. Like many young Indians, however, he chose a very different career path. Engineering took him to San Jose State University in California, followed by a promising career in Silicon Valley. On paper, everything looked perfect. Yet something never quite felt right. "I realised that I did not want to spend my whole life coding behind a computer. I wanted to be out in the field," he tells The Better India . The turning point came during a visit to a self-sustaining farm in Santa Cruz. Instead of being impressed by technology, he found himself drawn to simple outdoor work. "I remember working around the chicken coop and realising how much I enjoyed being outdoors, getting my hands into the work and being close to nature," he says with a laugh. Watching children explore the farm made the decision even clearer. "I could see myself in those children. They were fascinated by mud, insects and plants. I realised I wanted a life that kept me connected to the outdoors rather than one spent creating hardware." Soon afterwards, he left engineering behind. In 2010, Sohail joined the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), India's oldest natural history organisation. Over the next 13 years, he worked on conservation projects across the country, eventually becoming Assistant Director. In April 2023, he founded WildTales Foundation to continue that work. "People ask what motivated me to dedicate my life to conservation," he says. "For me, it never felt like a sacrifice. This is what I enjoy doing." The forest that changed everything One place transformed Sohail's understanding of conservation more than any other. Delhi's Asola Bhatti Wildlife Sanctuary, spread across nearly 32 square kilometres, is now one of the capital's largest green spaces. Few visitors realise that parts of it were once heavily scarred by mining. Working there taught him that bringing nature back is about far more than planting trees. Birds need it not only for drinking but also for bathing and keeping their feathers healthy. "People think it means planting thousands of trees. It is not that easy," he says. Instead, the real challenge is rebuilding the relationships that exist in nature. Which plants once grew there? Which insects depended on them? Which birds fed on those insects? "When those connections disappear," he explains, "the whole system begins to weaken." Another challenge soon became obvious. Finding native plants was surprisingly difficult. Most nurseries stocked ornamental species imported for decorative gardens, while local plants that naturally supported birds, butterflies and insects were rarely available. Rather than accepting that reality, Sohail and his colleagues decided to change it. They established a nursery dedicated entirely to native plants. Today, it produces nearly 10 lakh saplings every year, supplying restoration projects across Delhi and helping reintroduce species that had become difficult to find. The impact was visible within a few years. "When you bring back native plants, wildlife returns much faster than people expect. That is what fascinated me. You could actually see the difference." Why butterflies vanish when native plants disappear One lesson kept repeating itself through Sohail's years in the field: every plant supports life beyond itself . Most of us see a plant as something that makes a garden look greener. A butterfly sees it very differently. Many butterfly species lay their eggs only on specific native plants. Once the caterpillars hatch, they feed exclusively on those leaves. If those plants disappear, the butterflies often disappear with them. Many people remember childhood afternoons chasing butterflies through gardens, waking up to birdsong or watching moths gather around porch lights. Sohail points to the Common Mormon butterfly as an example. "Its caterpillars feed on curry leaf plants. If curry leaf disappears from an area, the butterfly won't simply shift to another ornamental plant. It can't." The same pattern plays out across nature. Native plants feed insects. Insects become food for birds. Birds disperse seeds that help forests regenerate. "When we replace native plants," Sohail says, "we're not just removing one species. We're breaking relationships that have developed over thousands of years." That is why, he believes, conservation isn't about planting more trees. It is about planting the right trees. Why beautiful gardens often fail wildlife Take a walk through most apartment complexes and gated communities. You'll probably find neatly trimmed lawns, ornamental palms and colourful imported flowers. They may look beautiful, Sohail says, but they rarely support much life. "We've been conditioned to value appearance over nature," he says. The biggest example is the manicured lawn. Lawns demand constant watering, mowing and fertilisers. Yet they provide very little food or shelter for butterflies, bees or birds. “Lawns are almost like green carpets. They look nice, but very little lives there.” Instead, Sohail believes our gardens should look a little more like nature. That means planting native trees, shrubs and grasses, letting fallen leaves become compost, and resisting the urge to trim every corner into perfect symmetry. Such gardens may appear less polished, but they quickly become alive with activity. Butterflies return to lay eggs. Bees begin visiting flowers. Birds arrive in search of insects and fruits. "The healthiest gardens aren't always the neatest," he says. "They're the ones where nature is allowed to do what it does best." Connecting Delhi's butterflies, one garden at a time After years of restoring forests, Sohail began asking himself a different question. Could cities become part of the solution too? That idea led to the Delhi Butterfly Corridor Project . Delhi's forests lie mostly around the city's edges. Between them stretch roads, buildings and concrete, making it difficult for butterflies and other pollinators to move safely across the landscape. Instead of creating one massive butterfly park, Sohail's team chose a different approach. They encouraged schools, parks, hospitals, residential societies and even individual households to grow small patches of butterfly-friendly native plants. Each garden may seem insignificant on its own. Together, they form stepping stones that allow butterflies to move across the city. One of the project's biggest successes came from a Government Senior Secondary School in RK Puram. Students planted native host plants, documented butterfly species and transformed their campus into an outdoor classroom. The project ended up changing more than just the garden. Children began observing insects instead of ignoring them. They created information boards, recorded species and became active participants in conservation. The initiative was so successful that the teacher leading it received the Best Teacher Award in 2022 . "When children start noticing butterflies," Sohail says, "they begin asking questions. That's where conservation really begins." 5 simple ways to welcome birds and butterflies back The good news, Sohail says, is that you don't need a large garden to help wildlife. A balcony, terrace or even a few pots can make a difference. Most of us see a plant as something that makes a garden look greener. A butterfly sees it very differently. 1. Skip chemical pesticides The biggest change starts with what not to use. "If we kill every insect we see, we also wipe out the insects that birds, butterflies and bees depend on," Sohail explains. Healthy gardens regulate themselves. Homemade compost and healthy soil encourage earthworms, microbes and beneficial insects that naturally keep pests in check. 2. Grow native plants The plants we choose decide which birds and butterflies visit our homes. Sohail recommends starting with species that naturally grow in your region. Curry leaf, lemon, milkweed ( Calotropis ), pattharchatta and native flowering climbers like desi madhumalti are excellent choices for butterflies. Instead of highly modified ornamental flowers, he suggests native marigolds and indigenous roses, which provide far more nectar for pollinators. “Many ornamental plants have been bred mainly for appearance. Native flowers still provide food for the insects that need them.” 3. Plant for birds, not just butterflies As butterflies return, birds soon follow. Fruit-bearing native plants such as mulberry, karonda and phalsa offer food, while grains like bajra and jowar attract seed-eating birds. "The greater the variety of plants," Sohail says, "the greater the variety of life your garden can support." 4. Keep water outside all year A simple bowl of water can become a lifeline. Birds need it not only for drinking but also for bathing and keeping their feathers healthy. "Don't wait for peak summer," he says. "Keep water available throughout the year." 5. Let nature be a little untidy Perhaps the hardest lesson is resisting the urge to keep everything perfectly neat. A few fallen leaves, wild grasses and naturally growing plants create shelter for insects and improve soil health. "Nature knows what it's doing. Sometimes the best thing we can do is step back and let it grow." A change that begins at home People often tell Sohail that wildlife belongs in forests, not cities. He couldn't disagree more. "Delhi has more than 400 bird species. Mumbai is home to around 70 leopards. Bengaluru still has leopards on its outskirts, and Bhopal shares its landscape with tigers," he says. "Wildlife is already around us. The question is whether we're making room for it." Every native plant added to a balcony, every pesticide-free garden and every bowl of water placed outside creates another safe stop for birds, butterflies and insects trying to survive in growing cities. On their own, these actions may seem small. Together, they can transform neighbourhoods. 'Make space for yourself too' Sohail believes conservation isn't only about protecting wildlife. It's also about rebuilding our own connection with nature. He encourages families to spend more time outdoors, whether in a forest, a neighbourhood park or simply in their own garden. "We are animals of the forest," he says. "Being surrounded by green is good not only for our physical health but also for our mental wellbeing." His favourite advice has little to do with gardening. Birds arrive in search of insects and fruits. "If you're creating a butterfly garden, make space for yourself in it too. Put a chair there. Have your morning tea there. Sit with your family. The more time you spend outdoors, the more you'll notice the life around you." Perhaps that's where change truly begins. Not through grand conservation campaigns, but through everyday choices — planting a native sapling, leaving out a bowl of water, or watching a butterfly settle on a curry leaf plant. The windscreens of our childhood may never again be covered with insects. But every Indian home has the chance to become a small refuge for nature. A balcony filled with native plants, a chemical-free garden or even a single water bowl can help birds, butterflies and bees find their way back. And if enough homes make that choice, the next generation may once again grow up thinking birdsong and butterflies are an ordinary part of everyday life — exactly as they should be.
